awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Teaching Engineering Design with a Contextual Perspective
awd_abstract_narration:
This project aims to serve the national interest by improving students’ understanding of how social, cultural, economic, and political systems can inform their engineering designs. Traditionally, engineering design courses have focused primarily on the technical specifications and requirements of a design without full consideration of the wider context in which they will be used. There is also a lack of engineering design courses in the middle two years of a typical engineering curriculum. This leads to a gap in learning design principles and skills for students between their first design course and the final capstone design course.  The project plans to develop, implement, refine, and evaluate engineering design courses for second and third year students at the University of Illinois-Chicago and the University of Texas-San Antonio. The courses should help students learn how to conduct in-depth analyses of the implications of design choices for society using historical and current examples of engineering design. This project intends to develop an instructional framework for the middle years of engineering programs' courses along with instructional materials for those courses. Using interviews and student surveys, the project will assess the impact of the courses on students. Project results will be disseminated to engineering educators through professional development workshops.

The goal of this project is to help students learn how to consider social, cultural, economic, and political factors during the engineering design process. This project is based on Critical Consciousness theory which suggests that students need to develop an awareness of inequitable societal conditions that can occur due to engineering design decisions. A new teaching framework for engineering design in the middle years will be developed and refined so that engineering design includes a contextual perspective. The goals for the new engineering design course are: (1) to empower students to be more socially and critically driven engineers, (2) to help students learn about the engineering design process from a Critical Consciousness perspective, and (3) to help students become validated in their aspirations to pursue an engineering career. An inter-group dialogue approach will be used in the course to establish communication relationships, facilitate dialogue, and encourage collaborations between students. This study will address two research questions: (1) What teaching strategies are most helpful in developing students’ critical consciousness through an engineering design course? (2) How and in what ways do the programmatic features of the project impact students’ learning of engineering design and engineering identity development? The project team will use quantitative and qualitative methods to analyze data from classroom observations, course artifacts, and student surveys. The NSF IUSE: EHR Program supports research and development projects to improve the effectiveness of STEM education for all students. Through the Engaged Student Learning track, the program supports the creation, exploration, and implementation of promising practices and tools.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project developed and launched a mid-year engineering design course that integrates contextual perspectives into engineering design. The course was successfully implemented at two higher education institutions: the University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA) and the University of Illinois Chicago (UIC). These campuses, with large populations of first-generation college students, provided a rich environment for testing and refining the curriculum. The course was first offered in spring 2023. The pedagogical approach of the course encouraged students to understand and critically examine contextual dimensions of engineering through their work as engineers. To achieve this, we created and refined a curriculum that teaches engineering design alongside topics such as moral and social responsibility, ethics, and accessibility. We partnered with community-based nonprofit organizations to give students hands-on experience designing solutions that serve real-world needs. We also used intergroup dialogue, reflection, multimodal literacy practices, and Model-Eliciting Activities (MEAs) to foster a contextualized understanding of engineering design.

The objectives of this project were:

  1. Develop a curricular intervention that connects engineering design processes to contextual perspectives of engineering
  2. Identify the core features of the curriculum that support and mediate interest in and knowledge of engineering through contextual perspectives
  3. Support students’ development of contextual perspectives in the classroom through continued support, reflection, and action
  4. Provide learning experiences for students that focus on the development of contextual perspectives in engineering

The project produced the following outcomes:

  1. The course impacted a total of 35 undergraduate students at UIC and 109 undergraduate students at UTSA. Four graduate students were trained in teaching and research methods through the project, and one undergraduate student was trained in teaching methods through participation in the development of the course.
  2. Undergraduate students who took the course developed a deeper understanding of how engineering impacts and is impacted by social systems. Students engaged with engineering as a social and human activity with consequences for different communities.
  3. Undergraduate students had opportunities to examine issues that are rarely discussed explicitly in engineering courses, including social responsibility, accessibility, and the ethical dimensions of risk assessment. Intergroup dialogue provided opportunities for students to openly discuss these issues, consider perspectives different from their own, and reflect on their responsibilities as engineers.
  4. The course provided another opportunity for undergraduate students to engage with engineering design early in their academic careers, addressing a gap that exists in several engineering fields across the nation. The project also provided evidence that authentic, open-ended design experiences can help students develop a more integrated understanding of engineering design.
  5. Undergraduate students who might otherwise feel disconnected from engineering found opportunities to develop renewed purpose and motivation to persist in the field. The course provided students with opportunities to connect engineering design to issues and problems that have meaning in their communities and society.
  6. The project demonstrated that integrating Model-Eliciting Activities (MEAs) into first-year engineering courses can effectively support students’ understanding of the engineering design process by engaging them in authentic, open-ended problem-solving tasks. MEAs provided students with opportunities to develop, test, and refine models while considering multiple approaches to engineering problems.
  7. The instructional framework developed through this project was shared with engineering educators through presentations and workshops at several engineering education conferences, as well as invited presentations at universities. These activities allowed the project team to disseminate project findings and provide professional development to more than 50 faculty members. 
  8. The project demonstrated that integrating engineering design, disciplinary literacy, and dialogue can support students’ development of critical consciousness and their understanding of engineering as a sociotechnical practice. Findings from the three-year implementation indicate that students engaged consistently with sociotechnical concepts and developed greater capacity to examine the consequences of engineering decisions.
  9. Faculty were introduced to an integrated method of teaching engineering that emphasizes social responsibility and contextual awareness, enabling them to connect technical design principles with their broader social, ethical, and human implications. This approach encouraged faculty to frame engineering education as a means for fostering responsible innovation and community-oriented problem solving.
  10. The project contributed to the development of engineering disciplinary literacy by demonstrating that critical consciousness can be integrated into engineering design rather than treated as an additional or peripheral skill. The project showed how engineering cases, reflection, dialogue, and critical literacy practices can help students learn to interpret and evaluate engineering decisions within their broader social contexts.
  11. The project demonstrated that the instructional approach can be adapted across different institutional contexts and levels of the engineering curriculum. The intervention was implemented at both first-year and mid-level courses and provided a framework that can be incorporated into existing courses through modules, design activities, reflection, and structured dialogue.
